opus-5.5.text:
I think it's possible, but it won't be a straight line, and it won't come from simply adding more of the same.

Tesla has done something very impressive. It has millions of cars on the road collecting data every day, and it has gone end to end: camera in, control out, with a large neural network in the middle. That data flywheel is a real advantage. From L2 to L2+, and even to what people call "supervised full self-driving," the experience has improved dramatically. As a driver assistance system it's among the best in the world.

But L4 is a different kind of problem. At L2, the human is the safety backup. At L4, the system is responsible. There's no driver to catch the mistake. So the question isn't whether the car drives well 99% of the time. The question is the long tail: the one-in-a-million or one-in-ten-million event. Fog, glare, a strange construction zone, a child running out behind a truck. In that regime, the bar goes from "better than average" to "provably and consistently much safer than humans," and you have to show that to regulators and to society.

Here I have some reservations about a pure-vision approach. Cameras are cheap and very rich in information, and humans drive with two eyes, so the argument has logic. But machines don't have to be limited to human senses. LiDAR and radar give you redundancy, direct depth, and robustness in bad weather or at night. Their cost has dropped by orders of magnitude, and in China a LiDAR now costs a few hundred dollars. For L4, I believe redundancy matters more than elegance. When you're responsible for safety, you want multiple independent ways of seeing the world.

The second point is that end-to-end models are powerful but harder to interpret and verify. When something goes wrong, you need to understand why, and you need guarantees, not just statistics. So I think the industry, Tesla included, will move toward a combination: large end-to-end or foundation models for generalization, plus some structured safety layer, simulation and world models to generate the long-tail cases you can't collect on real roads, and possibly vehicle-to-infrastructure cooperation.

So my assessment is this: the L2+ path is a very good way to accumulate data and capability, and it may reach L4 in limited areas and conditions. The robotaxi effort shows they are trying. But going from "it works most of the time" to "no one in the driver's seat, at scale, everywhere" takes the last few nines of reliability, and those last nines are the hardest. I would not bet against Elon, he has surprised people many times. But I think the winning L4 systems will be multi-sensor, with redundancy, heavy use of simulation, and close work with regulators. Whether that comes from the L2+ direction or the robotaxi-first direction, the two paths are converging.

r001.rationale: The response says L2 relies on a human safety backup and L4 cannot, but it does not state that this design assumption is why Musk’s current FSD cannot operate as a robotaxi.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to separate two questions. One is whether Musk's approach is impressive as engineering, and the answer is clearly yes. Pure vision, end-to-end neural networks, a fleet of millions of cars collecting data every day, and the ability to push software updates to that whole fleet overnight. That is a very powerful flywheel, and no one else has it at that scale.

The other question is whether that path leads naturally to L4, and here I am more cautious. L2+ and L4 are not two points on the same line. They are different products. In L2+, the human is the safety redundancy. When the system is unsure, it hands over, and the driver absorbs the long tail. In L4, there is no one to hand over to. The system itself has to be the redundancy. So the standard you are measured against changes completely. It is no longer "better than a human on average." It is "safe enough that a company is willing to take legal responsibility for every trip with no one behind the wheel."

That gap is about the last one or two percent of cases, and that is exactly where the hardest problems live. Unusual weather, sensor failure, construction zones, a policeman waving you through a red light. With a camera-only stack you have fewer independent sources of truth, so when the vision model is wrong, you have less to fall back on. That is why Waymo and the serious Chinese players kept lidar and radar, not because they do not believe in AI, but because redundancy is what certification and liability demand.

Having said that, I would not bet against Tesla's data advantage over the long run. Data plus compute has solved many problems people thought needed hand-crafted solutions. If their end-to-end models keep improving at the current rate, the economics of their approach become very attractive, because the hardware is cheap and already deployed. My honest view is that they will get to very strong L2+ faster than anyone, they will reach L4 in limited geofenced areas with some remote support, and true unrestricted L4 everywhere will take longer than Musk says, as it always has. The question is not whether the approach can reach L4. It is how much time, how many regulatory battles, and how much redundancy they will eventually have to add along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says L2+ relies on a human to take over and contrasts that with L4, but it does not state that FSD currently cannot operate as a robotaxi.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but it’s not simply a matter of making L2+ a little better. At L2, the driver is still responsible and has to be ready to take over. At L4, within a defined operating domain, the system has to handle the driving task and respond safely when something goes wrong. That is a fundamental change in responsibility and in the engineering requirements.

The strength of Musk’s approach is the potential to learn from a large fleet and improve the system through that feedback. The question is whether those improvements can deliver the reliability needed for driverless operation. Driving well in most situations is one thing; handling rare, difficult situations safely, without a human fallback, is another.

So I wouldn’t rule out that path. But I would judge it by demonstrated safety in a clearly defined operating domain, rather than assume that progress in L2+ automatically takes you to L4.

r001.rationale: The response says an L2 driver must be ready to take over, but it does not state that this design assumption is why Musk’s FSD cannot currently operate as a robotaxi.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but it’s not simply a matter of making L2+ progressively better until it becomes L4. There’s a change in responsibility. With L2+, the driver is still responsible and must be ready to intervene. At L4, within the system’s defined operating conditions, the vehicle has to handle the situation even when a human doesn’t take over.

So I would separate two questions: how capable is the driving model, and how do you demonstrate that the whole system is safe enough to operate without supervision? Musk’s approach has a potential advantage in the amount of driving data and the speed of iteration. But the difficult part is the long tail—rare situations, unusual road conditions, and failures that you may not encounter in ordinary driving.

I wouldn’t rule out that path reaching L4. But I’d judge it by reliable driverless operation within clearly defined conditions, rather than by how impressive a supervised drive looks. The last stretch requires more than better driving performance; it requires a convincing safety case.

r001.rationale: The response says that L2+ leaves responsibility with a driver who must be ready to intervene, but it does not state that this design assumption is why Musk’s FSD currently cannot operate as a robotaxi.
